# Article Ordered CoPt oxygen reduction catalyst with high performance and durability

An oxygen reduction reaction catalyst composed of core-shell CoPt nanoparticles possessing an ordered Co–Pt core and Pt shell shows excellent performance and durability in fuel cell testing.

## Article Ordered CoPt oxygen reduction catalyst with high performance and durability

Yung-Tin Pan,1,5 Dongguo Li,1 Shubham Sharma,2 Chenyu Wang,1 Michael J. Zachman,3

Evan C. Wegener,4 A. Jeremy Kropf,4 Yu Seung Kim,1 Deborah J. Myers,4 Andrew A. Peterson,2

David A. Cullen,3,* and Jacob S. Spendelow1,6,*

SUMMARY A high-performance and durable polymer electrolyte membrane fuel cell cathode catalyst composed of an ordered L10–CoPt core and a thin Pt shell was designed and prepared. Under practical fuel cell membrane electrode assembly testing conditions, the cathode catalyst showed an outstanding initial mass activity of 0.6 A/mgPt, which satisﬁes the U.S. Department of Energy performance target while also meeting the durability target of less than 40% loss in mass activity after 30,000 accelerated stress test voltage cycles. The high structural stability of the L10–CoPt@Pt-shell catalyst was conﬁrmed by postmortem materials characterization, and the origin of this robustness was revealed by density functional theory calculations, where the barriers for diffusion of Co atoms were observed to be signiﬁcantly increased in the ordered intermetallic core.

## INTRODUCTION

New platinum-based catalysts continue to break records in electrochemical oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) activity under well-controlled rotating disk electrode (RDE) conditions,1–7 but the realization of these high activities in realistic membrane electrode assembly (MEA) testing remains an elusive goal. The substantial performance/ knowledge gap between RDE and MEA conditions can be attributed to the signiﬁ- cantly different environments, including differences in electrolyte, double-layer structure, speciﬁc ionic adsorption, reactant concentration, humidity, temperature, ionic transport, and gas and water transport.8,9 The increasing need for clean energy transportation solutions, including an increased emphasis on fuel cells for heavy duty vehicle applications where life cycle costs are dominated by fuel economy, makes attainment of high MEA performance and durability more important than ever.10

A durable cathode catalyst is urgently needed to enable commercialization of fuel cells and fuel cell vehicles, with a durability of 5,000–8,000 h and 25,000–30,000 h targeted for light duty and heavy duty vehicles, respectively.11 These durability requirements pose a great challenge for state-of-the-art catalysts based on disordered, solid solution Pt-Ni or Pt-Co alloys, which exhibit high activity but poor stability. Leaching of base metals from these alloy catalysts can extend throughout the catalyst particles, rapidly degrading ORR performance.1,4,5,7,12–15 To survive for longer times under more corrosive MEA operating conditions, as we will show, a stronger bond between Pt and the alloying base metal atoms, along with atomic-level ordering that eliminates low-barrier pathways for base metal diffusion, are necessary. Such interactions can be achieved by the formation of intermetallic ordered structures where metallic bonds become covalent like.16 The formation of

Fuel cells with high power density and high durability could contribute to the realization of net zero carbon emissions in the transportation sector. The catalyst reported here, which uses atomiclevel ordering to stabilize Co within the intermetallic CoPt lattice, achieves higher Co retention and better durability compared with conventional CoPt catalysts. The limited reports on Pt–Ni based intermetallic catalysts so far indicate that these catalysts suffer from extensive sintering during the annealing process17,18 with electrochemical surface areas (ECSA) in the range of 20–30 m2/gPt.19,20 In contrast, Pt–Co-based catalysts, also promising for polymer electrolyte membrane fuel cell cathodes,13,21–27 show much stronger retention in the measured ECSA, ranging from 45 to 65 m2/gPt after the high temperature phase transformation process.

In previous work by Sun et al., a 10-nm L10–CoPt nanoparticle catalyst showed a mass activity of 0.56 A/mgPt with little loss after 30,000 catalyst accelerated stress test (AST) cycles under MEA testing conditions.28 Although this intermetallic catalyst met mass activity and durability targets, it exhibited low performance at high current density, resulting in a power density too low for transportation applications. This issue likely stemmed from the low ECSA of 27 m2/gPt, which could contribute to high local oxygen transport losses,29–31 along with low metal loading on the high surface area carbon support, which could cause water ﬂooding of the resulting thick electrode. Based on previous work by Kongkanand et al.,30 the local oxygen transport resistance of these large particles would be approximately 2 times higher compared with the commercial catalyst composed of carbon-supported 2- to 3-nm Pt particles.

In this study, we demonstrate the strategic design of new L10–CoPt ORR catalysts that meet U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) performance and durability targets in MEAs. High mass activity was achieved through a combination of small particle size and high Co content in the L10–CoPt lattice, which induced beneﬁcial compressive strain on the surface Pt atoms. Durability was signiﬁcantly enhanced by the formation of a core@shell catalyst exhibiting an ordered intermetallic-structured core and a Pt shell (hereafter referred to as the L10–CoPt@Pt-shell catalyst). Finally, to ensure high performance with minimized mass transport losses, the average diameter of L10–CoPt@Pt-shell catalyst particles was purposely controlled so as not to exceed 4 nm.29 With a cathode loading of 0.1 mgPt/cm2, the initial mass activity measured at 0.9 V under H2/O2 was 0.6 mA/mgPt. The mass activity loss was 40% after 30,000 catalyst AST cycles. In addition, the MEA exhibited an impressive H2/air performance of 0.38 A/cm2 at 0.8 V and a power output of 0.87 W/cm2 at 0.67 V (80C, 100% RH, 150 kPaabs), a voltage widely considered to be compatible with heat rejection limitations in light duty vehicles.29 This unique combination of ultrahigh activity and stability enables the catalyst to simultaneously meet DOE performance and durability targets for both catalysts and MEAs, making it a leading contender for deployment in light duty and heavy duty fuel cell vehicle applications.

Finally, to explore the origin of the experimentally observed high durability of the ordered CoPt structures, we turned to density functional theory (DFT) to calculate Co diffusion barriers in L10 and fcc CoPt geometries with systematically introduced disorder. The DFT calculations showed that a high degree of order in the core stabilizes Co, which otherwise is known to leach out of CoPt particles over time. The exceptional performance and durability of the catalyst reported here highlight the attractive dual functionality of the ordered L10–CoPt structure in activity and stability enhancement through strengthened Co–Pt bonds and elimination of low-barrier diffusion pathways. When incorporated in MEAs, this catalyst provides a remarkable combination of high power density and high durability that is unmatched in existing literature reports (Table S1).

## RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Three types of catalyst were compared in this study, including Pt, alloy-CoPt, and L10–CoPt@Pt-shell particles, all of which were supported on carbon (Vulcan XC- 72). The L10–CoPt@Pt-shell nanoparticle catalyst was prepared using a Co wet impregnation approach with commercially available Pt/C as a starting material, followed by high-temperature annealing to form an ordered L10 lattice and acid leaching to form a Pt shell. Figure 1A shows a high-angle annular dark-ﬁeld scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) micrograph of an as-prepared catalyst particle exhibiting the anticipated intermetallic core@Pt shell structure. The d-spacing of lattice fringes observed correspond to the (110) superlattice diffraction peaks at 33 2-theta that originate from the ordered intermetallic structure (Figure 1B). The powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) pattern of the catalyst closely matches the reference peaks calculated from the L10–CoPt unit cell except for the broad peak at 25, which corresponds with the Vulcan XC-72 carbon support (Figure 1B). In addition, the relatively weaker superlattice peaks are a key feature for the core-shell structure (Figure 1B, marked by *). Since the shell layer is not composed of an ordered structure, the intensity ratio between the superlattice peaks and lattice peaks appears lower than it would for a fully ordered structure. This can be further explained in Figure 1C, which is a zoomed-in view of the highlighted region of the inset scheme in Figure 1B. The (110) diffraction, which is forbidden for the fcc structure, is only produced by the ordered core (orange shaded area in Figure 1C). Whereas the intensity of (220) diffraction at 70 2-theta is a sum of the contribution from the ordered core and the Pt shell. As a result, the diffraction peaks from the whole particle, i.e., including both blue-shaded and orange shaded area, seemed to be much stronger compared with the superlattice peaks from the core.

The Fourier transforms of the Pt L3-edge extended X-ray absorption ﬁne structure (EXAFS) spectra and the ﬁts of these Fourier transforms to obtain coordination numbers and bond distances clearly reveal signiﬁcant differences in the coordination of Pt atoms in the L10–CoPt@Pt-shell, L10–CoPt, and alloy-CoPt samples as compared with that of a pure Pt sample (Figure S1). To simultaneously achieve high mass activity and high power performance, the growth of catalyst particle size during the high temperature annealing step must be minimized. As a result, sophisticated strategies have been reported to inhibit sintering of CoPt nanoparticles.28,32 However, by avoiding excessive metal content and using robust impregnation methods to provide strong particle-support interactions, we have eliminated the need for such strategies in the synthesis of our L10–CoPt. Our synthetic approach provides a simple and scalable method to produce L10–CoPt@Pt-shell with a number average diameter of 3.56 G 1.40 nm based on STEM analysis (Figure S2).

The crystal lattice of the as-prepared catalyst particles was characterized by PXRD (Figures 2A and S3), showing fcc-type packing for the Pt and alloy-CoPt catalysts.

Successful alloying was conﬁrmed by the rightward shift of the alloy catalyst diffraction peaks relative to the pure Pt catalyst peaks. In addition, the similar peak positions of the alloy-CoPt and L10–CoPt@Pt-shell catalyst indicate a similar level of lattice contraction of the 2 samples, i.e., the Pt atoms in the shell layer are experiencing similar levels of compressive strain in the 2 types of CoPt catalyst. The averaged particle size distribution determined from STEM micrographs shows an average diameter of 3.56 G 1.40 nm, 3.35 G 1.53 nm, and 3.50 G 1.23 for the L10–CoPt@Pt-shell, alloy-CoPt, and Pt particles, respectively (Figures S2, S4, and S5). Such similarity in particle size and distribution is a prerequisite for studying the effects of composition on performance and durability under MEA testing conditions. Figure 2B shows the mass activity of the three catalysts tested under H2/O2 at 0.9 V under 150 kPaabs H2/O2 according to DOE protocols (Figure S6). The mass activity at beginning of life (BOL) was 0.60 A/mgPt for both CoPt catalysts, well above the DOE target of 0.44 A/mgPt. The comparable performance can be attributed to the similar particle size and similar compressive strain experienced by the surface Pt atoms. The Pt catalyst, in contrast, showed a BOL mass activity of 0.29 A/mgPt. After the catalyst AST (30,000 cycles, see experimental procedures section for details), the mass activity of the L10–CoPt@Pt-shell catalyst was 0.36 A/mgPt, which was substantially higher compared with the alloy catalyst (0.27 A/mgPt). The loss in mass activity after 30,000 catalyst AST cycles meets the DOE durability target of 40% or less loss in mass activity. In contrast, the alloy catalyst suffered a 56% mass activity loss. Figures 2C and 2D show the polarization curves of the three catalysts tested under H2/air at BOL and after 30,000 AST cycles, hereafter denoted as end of life (EOL). The L10–CoPt@Pt-shell catalyst showed the highest performance both in the kinetic and ohmic regions with a high current density of 1.63 A/cm2 at 0.6 V and 1.30 A/cm2 at the heat rejection limit of 0.67 V (Figure 2C). When tested at 250 kPaabs, the L10–CoPt@Pt-shell showed a performance of 1.1 W/cm2, well exceeding the DOE target of 1 W/cm2 (Figure S7). At the BOL, the alloy catalyst showed comparable performance, in good agreement with the BOL mass activity measurements. The difference between the polarization curves of the L10– CoPt@Pt-shell and the alloy catalyst became more signiﬁcant after 30,000 cycles of catalyst AST, matching the trend observed in the mass activity measurements (Figure 2D). The L10–CoPt@Pt-shell catalyst demonstrated higher durability compared with the alloy catalyst, exhibiting a current density of 1.49 A/cm2 at 0.6 V and 1.17 A/cm2 at the 0.67 V heat rejection limit after 30,000 AST cycles. In addition to mass activity and durability targets measured in H2/O2, the DOE has also set performance and durability targets speciﬁed under H2/air at 0.8 V and 0.8 A/cm2. The 0.8-V performance in Figures 2C and 2D is summarized in Figure 2E. At BOL, L10–CoPt@Pt-shell catalyst showed a current density of 0.38 A/cm2, well exceeding the DOE target of 0.3 A/cm2 with a loss of only 32% to 0.26 A/cm2 after catalyst AST, while alloy-CoPt showed a loss of 48% (0.35 A/cm2 to 0.18 A/cm2). The voltage loss at 0.8 A/cm2 of the L10–CoPt@Pt-shell catalyst was only 26 mV (758– 732 mV), satisfying the DOE target of 30 mV, whereas the alloy-CoPt showed a 37 mV loss (0.745–0.708 V) (Figure 2F). The 33% ECSA loss for the L10–CoPt@Pt-shell was also the mildest among all catalysts tested (Figures 2G and S8).

A detailed analysis was performed to decipher the origin of the high performance and durability of the L10–CoPt@Pt-shell from a materials perspective. To further complement the experimentally observed high durability of the L10– CoPt@Pt-shell catalyst compared with the disordered alloy catalyst, an atomistic model using DFT was used to systematically study Co stability in CoPt bulk systems with increasing degrees of disorder. At the catalytic surface, the loss of non-noble elements like Co is mainly attributed to dissolution under harsh fuel cell conditions.34–36 For core-shell structures containing a Pt shell, and assuming that only Co atoms on the surface can dissolve into the solution, dissolution must be accompanied by internal diffusion for further degradation over time. While diffusion in solids can occur through interstitial, collective, or vacancy-mediated mechanisms, the lattermost is recognized as the most dominant mechanism for diffusion of atoms of similar size within metals and alloys.37–40

To study the effect on Co stability within the core with increasing randomness, a vacancy mediated diffusion model was therefore considered to compute diffusion barriers for Co diffusion into vacancies, as shown in Figure 4. We hypothesize that the degree of disorder or concentration in the local environment can inﬂuence the diffusion energetics which can result in degradation of the core over time. This hypothesized change in the diffusion barriers was studied by introducing systematic randomness in the local environment through 2 different approaches, viz. replacing and swapping. For randomness through replacement, a change in the composition of the super-cell (i.e., the simulated cell) was allowed by replacing one element type with another. For randomness through swapping, the composition of the super-cell was kept the same (i.e., 50:50 in Co:Pt) while allowing for the interchange of atomic

As shown in the schematic (Figure 5), for vacancy mediated diffusion in fcc and L10 bulk, an atom must diffuse through the space between a set of 4 atoms, referred to here as the bridge atoms. For a symmetric reaction pathway (i.e., for similar initial and ﬁnal states), the local environment of the diffusing element prior and post diffusion must remain the same, suggesting that only the composition of the bridge atoms can inﬂuence the diffusion barrier. This was conﬁrmed through the DFT-calculated trend, showing a decrease in Co diffusion barrier with increasing Co concentration in the bridge atoms, as shown in Figure 4 (and Figures S13 and S14). Similarly, for asymmetric reaction pathways, the change in local environment of the initial and ﬁnal state must also inﬂuence the diffusion barrier. In fact, for asymmetric reaction pathways (highlighted as F and G in Figure S13) the reverse barriers for diffusion (Figure S15) are much lower than the forward barriers, implying that Co would prefer to stay in Co rich environments with increasing degree of disorder. Though the diffusion of Co through Co vacancies seems to be predominant in CoPt alloys owing to the greater ease of dissolution of Co compared with Pt, we also calculated the diffusion barriers of Co through Pt vacancies. As shown in Figure S16A, a decrease in the Co diffusion barrier with increasing Co percent in the bridge atoms was observed for Co diffusion through Pt vacancies. For Co diffusing in the Co vacancies, we observed that the ordered structures corresponded to the systems with the highest Co diffusion barriers. This suggests that a high degree of order is essential to ensure higher kinetic stability of Co. Similarly, for Co diffusion through Pt vacancies, we observed that disordered structures could result in lower Co diffusion barriers compared with the ordered structure. These computational results are in good agreement with our experimental observation that L10–CoPt stabilizes Co more effectively than fcc-CoPt.

Conclusions An ORR catalyst meeting the DOE fuel cell catalyst and MEA targets was strategically designed and prepared through the optimization of the crystal ordering and size distribution of core-shell CoPt catalyst. The prepared sub-4-nm catalyst was composed of an ordered L10 core surrounded by a Pt shell. This catalyst demonstrated outstanding performance and durability under MEA testing conditions with a mass activity of 0.6 A/mgPt, a high power density of 0.986 W/cm2 at 0.6 V under H2/air at 150 kPaabs, and only 40% mass activity loss after 30,000 catalyst AST cycles. The high performance is attributed to enhanced ORR kinetics because of the compressive strain applied on the surface Pt-shell and the relatively large ECSA exposed by the sub-4-nm catalyst particles. Materials and chemicals Materials used include platinum on carbon (TEC10V10E and TEC10V20E, TKK); cobalt (II) acetylacetonate (Co(acac)2, 97%; Sigma-Aldrich); chloroform (Sigma- Aldrich); methanol (certiﬁed ACS; Fisher Scientiﬁc); isopropanol (certiﬁed ACS; Fisher Scientiﬁc); n-propanol (spectroscopy grade, Fisher Scientiﬁc); acetic acid (glacial, Fisher Scientiﬁc); deionized-water (18.2W, Q-series, Millipore); nitrogen (N2, UHP grade, Airgas); forming gas (6% H2 balanced with Ar, Airgas); oxygen (O2, UHP grade, Airgas); Naﬁon ionomer solution (D2020, Ion Power); Naﬁon membrane (NR211, Ion Power); gas diffusion layer (Sigracet 29BC, SGL). Preparation of L10–CoPt@Pt-shell nanoparticle catalyst The process of preparing L10–CoPt@Pt-shell nanoparticle catalyst began with the preparation of L10–CoPt followed by selective surface etching and healing. Preparation of L10–CoPt nanocatalyst began by wet impregnation of cobalt precursors onto the commercial Pt/C catalyst (TEC10V10E). In a typical process, 100 mg Pt/C was dispersed in 25 mL of chloroform in a clean glass bottle via ultrasonication. After 1 h, the designated amount of Co(acac)2 (dissolved in chloroform, typically 5 mL) was introduced into the Pt/C-chloroform mixture and was kept under sonicating conditions for 30 min. To remove excess solvents, the mixture bottle was stirred under 300 rpm with a magnetic stir bar at open-cap conditions on a 70C magnetic hotplate stirrer for 2 h. The remaining thick solution/slurry was then transferred to a watch glass to allow the ﬁnal drying of the Co-impregnated Pt/C sample. To induce the alloying of Co and Pt and the further transformation into ordered L10 phase, the dry powders were thermally treated under a ﬂow of forming gas (6% H2 balanced with Ar) at 700C with a ramp rate of 10 C/min in a quartz tube furnace (Thermo- Lindberg Minimite). After 12 h of treatment at 700C, the samples were naturally cooled down under a ﬂow of forming gas. At room temperature, before exposure to air, the quartz tube was purged with N2 to prevent co-exposure of catalyst to H2 and air. The annealed sample was further treated with acetic acid in an ultrasonic bath at room temperature for 30 min to remove the non-alloyed Co species and ﬁnally washed by methanol. The washing included sonication of powder samples in methanol and separation by centrifugation for at least 3 repetitive cycles.

Materials characterization The materials presented in this work can be categorized into freshly prepared powders and post-fuel cell testing MEA samples. Both types of samples went through thorough examinations with PXRD and (S)TEM. PXRD was performed at Los Alamos National Lab with a Siemens D5000 diffractometer. Conventional bright ﬁeld TEM was performed at Los Alamos National Laboratory (Tecnai, FEI). Aberration-corrected STEM imaging and EDS mapping was executed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory on a probe-corrected JEOL NEOARM operated at 80 kV and equipped with dual 100-mm2 solid state detectors for EDS analysis.33 X-ray absorption measurements were made on the bending magnet beamline of the Materials Research Collaborative Access Team at the Advanced Photon Source, Argonne National Laboratory. Normalization and background subtraction were performed using standard procedures. The EXAFS coordination parameters were determined from simultaneous ﬁts in R-space of the magnitude of the Fourier transform of the k1-, k2-, and k3-weighted EXAFS. Theoretical phase shift and backscattering amplitude ﬁtting functions were calculated using the FEFF software.42 S0 2 was determined from the ﬁt of the Pt foil reference by ﬁxing the coordination numbers at the known values. The obtained value, 0.82, was held constant in the ﬁts of the samples.

The catalyst ink was composed of 24 mg catalyst powder mixed with 89 mg D2020 ionomer solution and 9.25 g DI-water/n-propanol solution. The ionomer to carbon ratio was 0.5 and the volumetric ratio of DI-water to n-propanol was 4:3. The mixture was stirred at 700 rpm for 10–20 min and placed in an ultrasonication bath with ice water for an additional 20 min. Fuel cell testing The fuel cell was assembled by sandwiching the prepared MEA in between 2 gas diffusion layers (GDL, 29BC) and ﬁxed inside the fuel cell hardware using polyurethane sheets as gaskets. The hardware was then screwed tight using a torque wrench with 10 lbf$inch intervals until reaching 50 lb$inch. The assembled cell was then connected to a fuel cell test station (Fuel Cell Technologies Inc.) for a simple break-in procedure at 0.6 V under H2/air (anode/cathode, 500/1,000 SCCM, 150 kPaabs, 80C, 100% RH) until a stable current had been reached. The cell further went through many cycles of conditioning, which includes ECSA measurements and 0 V potential holds under H2/N2 at 30C and 80C respectively; 0 V holds under H2/air at 80C; mass activity measurements under H2/O2 at 0.9 V; and polarization curve measurements under H2/air from 0.4 V to OCV. Conditioning cycles were repeated until the MEA performance stabilized. ECSA measurements were performed with both the hydrogen underpotential deposition (HUPD) and carbon monoxide stripping method. In both measurements, the cell was kept at 30C while the humidiﬁers at 80C under H2/N2 or H2/CO for 10 min, to allow the cell to reach equilibrium. For the HUPD measurements, cyclic voltammetry (CV) was applied to the cathode scanning from 0.08 V to 0.55 V for 7 cycles at a rate of 20 mV/s by a potentiostat (Biologic, SP-200). For CO stripping, the cathode was purged with N2 for 10 min to remove unadsorbed CO gas molecules. CV was then applied to the cathode scanning from 0.1 V to 1.1 V with a rate of 50 mV/s. Before mass activity measurements, the cell was kept at 0 V under H2/N2 while heated back to 80C. Once 80C was reached, the gas was changed to H2/air while keeping the cell voltage at 0 V for an additional 30 min. Mass activity measurements were performed under H2/O2 at 80C, 100% RH, 150kPaabs, and ﬂowrates of 500/1,000 SCCM. The cell was held at 0.6 V for 5 min to allow equilibration from the previous H2/N2 environment and stepped to 0.9 V and held for 15 min followed by a 1 min OCV and an HFR measurement. Polarization curves were measured by stepping the cell voltage from 0.4 V to 0.8 V, with a 0.05 V steps of 4-min durations, followed by 0.025 V steps to 0.9V and 2 ﬁnal steps at 0.91 V and OCV under H2/air, 100% RH, 500/1000 SCCM. Durability testing was performed using an AST in which the cell voltage was cycled between 0.60 and 0.95 V in a trapezoidal wave, with 0.5-s rise time and 2.5-s hold time, for 30,000 cycles. The durability test was performed at 80C under H2/N2, 200/200 SCCM, 150 kPaabs, 100% RH.

Computation details The ab initio electronic structure calculations in DFT were performed using a gridbased projector-augmented wave43,44 method with a plane wave (PW) basis set. The atomic models were created and manipulated in an atomic simulation environment.45 A PW cut-off of 550 eV with the revised Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof46

exchange-correlation functional was used. A k-point mesh of 10 3 10 3 10 was used for lattice optimization, while a 4 3 4 3 4 mesh was used for all the other calculations. Ferromagnetism of CoPt was considered by accounting for spin-polarization. The CoPt cores were modeled as periodic 2 3 2 3 2 super-cells containing a total of 32 atoms. A vacancy was created by deleting an atom in the super cell. For every vacancy meditated diffusion, the initial and ﬁnal states were allowed to geometrically optimize until the force on each atom in the super-cell converged to less than 0.05 eV/A˚ .
